statement: A solid is made of stacks of identical cubes on a 3-by-3 square base. From the front, the three columns, left to right, look 2, 3 and 1 cubes tall. From the right side, the three rows, front to back, look 3, 1 and 2 cubes tall. What is the greatest number of cubes the solid can contain?

choices.misconception: I found the smallest number of cubes that gives these two views, not the greatest.
I added the 6 cubes I can see from the front to the 6 cubes I can see from the side.
I made each stack as tall as the larger of its two view heights instead of the smaller one.
I made every one of the nine stacks 3 cubes tall, the tallest height in either view.

hints: Each stack is limited by two views at once.
Each stack is capped by the front-view height of its column and the side-view height of its row. For the most cubes, build every stack to the smaller of its two caps, then check both views.
Front row (limit 3): heights 2, 3, 1. Middle row (limit 1): 1, 1, 1. Back row (limit 2): 2, 2, 1.

solutions.reliable: Give each stack its column (front view) and its row (side view). Its height can be at most the smaller of the two view values. Front row, limit 3: heights 2, 3, 1, total 6. Middle row, limit 1: 1, 1, 1, total 3. Back row, limit 2: 2, 2, 1, total 5. Every column and every row still reaches its stated height, so both views are right, and the greatest total is 6 + 3 + 5 = 14. The transferable idea: two views only cap each stack at the smaller of its two readings, and filling every stack up to its cap gives the maximum.

whyOnTest: Views questions test whether you see that each view only caps a stack, so the most and the fewest cubes are different questions.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
